content: In women, ovulation typically causes an increase in BBT by approximately 0.5 to 1 degree Fahrenheit (or 0.25 to 0.5 degrees Celsius). Monitoring BBT is a method used to estimate the timing of ovulation. Women generally exhibit a biphasic temperature pattern, characterized by lower temperatures before ovulation and higher temperatures afterward. This biphasic pattern can be charted and utilized as part of fertility awareness methods. The biphasic pattern is hormonally driven. During the pre-ovulatory (follicular) phase of the menstrual cycle, elevated estrogen levels suppress BBT. After ovulation, the corpus luteum releases progesterone, which raises BBT. The temperature increase is most commonly observed the day after ovulation, though this can vary. BBT tracking can only estimate ovulation within a three-day window. If pregnancy does not occur, the corpus luteum disintegrates, leading to a drop in BBT that typically coincides with the onset of menstruation. If pregnancy does occur, the corpus luteum remains active and sustains elevated BBTs throughout the first trimester. After the first trimester, the placenta assumes the hormonal functions of the corpus luteum, and the woman’s body temperature returns to pre-ovulatory levels. In rare cases, the corpus luteum may form a cyst, which can cause prolonged elevation of BBT and delay menstruation for weeks or months until the cyst resolves. For women trying to conceive, regular menstrual cycles are often interpreted as a sign of normal ovulation, while irregular cycles may suggest ovulatory dysfunction. However, this is not always accurate. Many women with irregular cycles ovulate normally, and some with regular cycles may experience anovulation or luteal phase defects. By recording BBT, it is possible to confirm whether ovulation is occurring and to assess whether the luteal phase is of sufficient length to support a pregnancy. Pregnancy tests are not reliable until 1-2 weeks after ovulation. Knowing the approximate date of ovulation can help avoid false-negative pregnancy test results caused by testing too early. Additionally, 18 consecutive days of elevated BBT strongly indicate pregnancy. Tracking BBT is also a more precise method of estimating gestational age compared to relying on menstrual cycle dates. For women seeking to avoid pregnancy, BBT charting is a component of some fertility awareness methods. It can help identify the onset of post-ovulatory infertility. However, BBT only confirms that ovulation has already occurred; it does not predict ovulation. Since sperm can survive in the female reproductive tract for up to five days, predicting ovulation several days in advance is necessary to avoid pregnancy. BBT-based methods often incorporate rules similar to those of the Calendar Method to estimate the beginning of the pre-ovulatory fertile phase.
